question: Assume the JTB definition of Knowledge, which suggests that "Knowledge is a Justified True Belief". If our only available epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief, what are the two problems JTB runs into? Ignore Gettier problems.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two main problems seem to be (1) that justification itself must ultimately rest on something that is either already known or merely believed, which leaves no non-arbitrary stopping point for what counts as adequate support, and (2) that “truth” cannot be established from within the JTB framework alone without smuggling in an external criterion that is not itself a belief or knowledge state. This forces the account either to stipulate an unanalyzed foundation or to accept that many intuitively justified beliefs remain outside the definition.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two problems JTB runs into are that it collapses the distinction between knowledge and mere true belief whenever justification cannot be independently verified from within the agent's own mental states, and that it forces an all-or-nothing threshold on justification that either counts too many accidentally correct beliefs as knowledge or excludes too many ordinary well-supported beliefs, producing an unstable boundary between the two allowed epistemic states.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two problems JTB runs into here are (1) the difficulty of independently verifying that a belief is in fact true without already presupposing knowledge, and (2) the challenge of specifying a non-arbitrary standard for what counts as adequate justification when the only available states are knowledge and mere belief. The first issue arises because confirming truth seems to require a prior epistemic grip that JTB itself does not supply, while the second leaves justification standards either too permissive or reliant on external criteria the definition does not provide.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Given only Knowledge and Belief as available states, JTB seems to face two main difficulties: first, it offers no independent criterion for verifying the "truth" component without already presupposing knowledge, and second, it leaves open how agents could ever acquire the initial justified beliefs needed to bootstrap the whole account, risking an empty or vacuous theory of knowledge. This would make JTB either circular in its truth-checking or simply inapplicable to real cognitive agents.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The JTB account runs into two main difficulties when limited to knowledge and belief as epistemic states. First, justification appears to require an external or non-epistemic criterion (such as causal reliability or coherence with experience) that cannot itself be reduced to either knowledge or belief without circularity. Second, even with justification in place, the account still cannot guarantee that a true belief counts as knowledge in cases where the justification is merely accidentally connected to the truth, forcing an additional, non-JTB condition that the framework itself does not supply.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The JTB account, restricted to only knowledge and belief as epistemic states, faces two main difficulties. First, it struggles to provide a non-circular account of what makes a belief "justified," because any appeal to further beliefs simply re-describes the same relation without independent grounding. Second, it leaves unclear how we could ever confirm that a belief is actually true rather than merely believed to be true, since truth-assessment would itself have to be carried out using only the same two states and therefore risks collapsing into another layer of belief. These issues make the definition feel incomplete even before considering counterexamples such as Gettier cases.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: On a JTB analysis Knowledge = Justified + True + Belief. 

With only two epistemic boxes the four logically distinct combinations of
Justified / Unjustified and True / False have to be squeezed into
Knowledge and Belief.

* JTB  → Knowledge
* ~JTB → Belief

So Belief becomes a heterogeneous residue. Two of the residue cases are
epistemically interesting and they are made indistinguishable from each
other and from plain false/unjustified belief.

1. Justified false belief. A belief can be fully justified for the subject
and still be false. On JTB it is not Knowledge because it is not true,
so with the two-state taxonomy it must be counted as mere Belief. The
justification is therefore invisible in the taxonomy: an epistemically
responsible, well grounded false belief is lumped together with an
arbitrary, unjustified false belief.

2. Unjustified true belief. A belief can be true by accident, luck or
blind guess with no justification at all. On JTB it is not Knowledge
because it is not justified, so with the two-state taxonomy it must
again be counted as mere Belief. The truth of the belief is therefore
invisible in the taxonomy: an epistemically irresponsible true belief
is lumped together with a justified false belief.

In effect Belief has to do duty for both “justified but false” and
“true but unjustified”. The binary Knowledge / Belief taxonomy therefore
cannot keep apart epistemic virtue from epistemic luck and it cannot mark
the normative difference between a justified falsity and an unjustified
truth. That is the classic non-Gettier coarseness of JTB.

2.text:
With JTB Knowledge = J & T & B you get a tripartite structure for a
propositional attitude, justification, truth and belief.

If the only attitude labels you are allowed to use are Knowledge and
Ordinary Belief then every attitude that is not K must be put under B.
That forces B to be a disjunctive, heterogeneous catch-all.

* Justified false belief , J & ~T & B.
That attitude is not Knowledge because Knowledge entails truth. On the
binary scheme it can only be called Belief. Belief is then used for an
attitude that is in fact epistemically good, it is justified, in the
same class as unjustified, merely held false beliefs. The normative
difference between a rational false belief and an irrational false
belief is lost.

* Unjustified true belief, ~J & T & B.
That attitude is not Knowledge because Knowledge entails justification.
On the binary scheme it can only be called Belief. Belief is then used
for an attitude that is alethically good, it is true, in the same class
as false beliefs. The alethic difference between a lucky true belief and
a false belief is lost.

Hence Belief has to contain both justified beliefs that happen to be
false and true beliefs that happen to be unjustified.  The Knowledge /
Belief dichotomy cannot respect the independence of justification and
truth: you cannot mark off a justified belief that is false as a sui
generis rational but false state, nor can you mark off a true belief
that is unjustified as a sui generis lucky but epistemically worthless
state.  Belief becomes the heterogeneous class J&~T&B ∨ ~J&T&B ∨ ~J&~T&B,
and the tripartite analysis ceases to give a clean Knowledge vs mere
Belief partition. That is the independence problem of J and T that is
distinct from the Gettier problem of J & T & B that is still not
knowledge.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With JTB the 2 x 2 grid of truth and justification collapses into
Knowledge = J ∧ T ∧ B  and  Belief = ¬Knowledge.

That is you only have a positive epistemic state, Knowledge, and a negative residual state, Belief. On that dichotomy every non-knowledge is just ‘belief’,

* J ∧ T ∧ B = Knowledge
* J ∧ ¬T ∧ B = Belief
* ¬J ∧ T ∧ B = Belief
* ¬J ∧ ¬T ∧ B = Belief

so justification and truth are no longer independently trackable in the belief state.

Hence with only Knowledge vs Belief as primitive attitudes you lose the
two non-knowledge cells which are epistemically different.

1. Justified false belief. A belief can be properly justified and still be
false. JTB makes that a mere Belief, i.e. it is lumped together with
unwarranted belief. The epistemic value of being justified is thereby
erased once the belief turns out false, and justified false belief has
no distinct home in the taxonomy. In familiar terms this is the ‘justified
but wrong’ or ‘false lemma’ difficulty: you can be epistemically good
without knowing.

2. Unjustified true belief. A belief can be true by accident, luck,
guesswork, etc., with no justification at all. JTB also makes that a mere
Belief, i.e. it is lumped together with justified false belief and with
unjustified false belief. The epistemic defect of lacking justification is
thereby erased once the belief happens to be true. This is the ‘lucky
guess / true without warrant’ difficulty: you can be true without
knowing.

In effect Knowledge entails Belief but Belief does not entail Knowledge,
so with only the two attitudes available justified false belief and
unjustified true belief are indistinguishable from one another and from
unjustified false belief. The positive value of justification and the
positive value of truth are no longer separable states, which is why
knowledge is usually thought to be more than, and not just a species of,
mere belief. Gettier aside those are the classic truth-versus-justification
pressures on the tripartite analysis.

10.text:
With the tri-partite analysis knowledge is defined as a species of belief

K(p) := B(p) & T(p) & J(p)

If the only epistemic categories you allow are *belief* and *knowledge* the
J-clause cannot be cashed out in its own terms.

Justification of p has to be given in epistemic terms.  On the present
dichotomy that can only be given by citing another epistemic state,
either a belief or a knowledge. 

* If J(p) is cashed out by a further belief B(q) that is offered in support
of p, then J(q) is required, and J(q) is required by a further belief,
etc.  You get the familiar regress of justification: a belief never gets
off the ground because every justifier is itself a belief in need of a
justifier.  In the limit there is no non-infinite chain of B-states that
can ground p.

* If the regress is stopped by making the justifier itself a knowledge
state, J(p) is made to depend on K(q).  But K(q) is by definition B(q)&T(q)
&J(q), so the justifying state already contains a belief that itself
needs a justifier.  The justification of p is therefore made to depend
on the justification of q and you are back in the regress, or, if the
chain is closed, on p itself.  That is the vicious circularity / dogmatic
foundational alternative: either you allow an arbitrary, unjustified
basic belief / basic knowledge to stop the chain, i.e. dogmatism, or you
close the chain on itself.

That is why with only B and K in the stock the JTB analysis is forced to
coarse grain the belief space. An unjustified true belief and a justified
false belief are both just *B*, there is no epistemic place to mark them
off from mere opinion. In practice the system can only distinguish

* B & T & J = K
* B otherwise

so justified false belief and accidental true belief are indistinguishable
from unjustified false belief, and justification itself has no independent
state to be realised in. The regress / circularity dilemma is the
formal expression of that coarse graining.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With Knowledge = Justified + True + Belief and with only
Knowledge vs Belief as the live categories every state that fails to meet
all three conditions is forced into the single residual category Belief.

That forces a heterogeneous grab bag into Belief and the justification /
truth dimensions are lost.

1. Justified false belief. JTB is factive so a false belief can never be
knowledge even if it is ideally justified. On a Knowledge/Belief only
scheme a justified false belief is therefore just Belief. It is lumped
together with an unjustified false belief. The epistemic virtue of
justification is thereby erased: justified falsity and unjustified falsity
are indiscriminable as mere belief, even though the former is epistemically
much better than the latter.

2. Unjustified true belief. JTB is justification dependent so a true
belief that lacks adequate justification can never be knowledge. On a
Knowledge/Belief only scheme an unjustified true belief is therefore just
Belief. It is lumped together with justified false belief and with
unjustified false belief. The epistemic virtue of truth is thereby erased:
accidentally true belief is indiscriminable as mere belief from
justified false belief and from wholly unwarranted false belief, even
though it shares truth with knowledge and is epistemically better than
false belief.

Hence Belief becomes the disjunction of justified false + unjustified true
+ unjustified false, i.e. a non-uniform category. The JTB analysis is forced
to conflate epistemically distinct states – good justification/bad truth
and bad justification/good truth – because justification and truth can no
longer be tracked independently of the Knowledge/Belief dichotomy.

11.text:
With the JTB schema

K p  iff  Bp & p & Jp

`Jp` is not itself a state of believing or of knowing. If those are the only
states we allow, a justifier for p has to be cashed out in states of believing
or of knowing.

* Justification as knowledge. If Jp is to be other than vacuous it has to be
already known that p is justified. Then

K p iff K p is true and Bp

and the analysis is circular. Knowledge is analysed in terms of knowledge,
and the only way to block the circle is to make the justifier infallible,
i.e. to demand that a justifier be itself known infallibly. Knowledge then
becomes essentially circular / dogmatic.

* Justification as belief. If Jp is to be a belief then

K p iff Bp is true and Bp is believed by some further belief

i.e. knowledge is true belief based on belief. That makes justification
fallible and extrinsic to the state classified as K or B. You can then have
a true belief which counts as knowledge on the basis of a false, or even
unjustified, belief, and the justifying belief itself stands in need of a
justifier, etc.  In the absence of a distinct justified-belief state the
justification chain either regresses ad infinitum or is stopped by an
unjustified foundational belief.

The upshot in the bare K/B inventory is a collapse of the epistemic
landscape. There is no room in the inventory for a distinct state of
justified false belief and no room for a distinct state of true but
unjustified belief. A false belief is just a belief, whether it is
warranted or not, and a true belief is either Knowledge, if it is
justified, or a mere Belief, if it is not.  Justified false belief and
unjustified true belief are therefore not discriminable from bare belief,
so the JTB schema cannot do the work of distinguishing warranted from
unwarranted error on the one hand and lucky truth from warranted truth on
the other, and the justification clause can only be made intelligible at the
price of circularity or an infinite regress of beliefs. That is the
well known regress / circularity problem for the analysis of justification
and the consequent loss of a place for justified false belief / unjustified
true belief in a two-state taxonomy.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With Knowledge = Justified True Belief and Belief as the only residual
category the state “mere belief’’ is forced to do all the work that is left over
from JTB. That makes Belief a heterogenous dump and it removes any
epistemic place for two intuitively distinct situations.

1. Justified false belief, JFB. A belief can be properly justified and yet
false. On JTB it is not Knowledge because the truth condition fails, so with
only Knowledge / Belief as options it has to be counted as mere Belief.
Hence justified beliefs that are false are lumped together with unjustified,
irrational beliefs. We lose any way of marking the epistemic value of
justification when truth is absent.

2. Unjustified true belief, UTB. A belief can be true by luck or accident
and yet be wholly unjustified. On JTB it is not Knowledge because the
justification condition fails, so with only Knowledge / Belief as options it
has to be counted as mere Belief. Hence a lucky true belief is lumped
together with false beliefs. We lose any way of marking the epistemic defect
of lack of justification when truth is present.

In effect Belief has to be both justified and unjustified and both true and
false at once. Knowledge is thereby made too narrow – it excludes
justified false beliefs we want to count as epistemically good – and Belief
is made too broad – it conflates lucky true beliefs with bad false beliefs
and justified false beliefs with unjustified false beliefs. That is the
truth-gap / justification-gap that remains even once Gettier cases are set
aside.

4.text:
Under JTB the space of doxastic attitude + truth-value is in principle 2x2

Justified / Unjustified x True / False

JTB identifies one of the four cells with Knowledge

J T = Knowledge
J F = ?
U T = ?
U F = ?

If the only attitudinal kinds you allow are Knowledge and Belief then J F, U T and U F all have to be classified as mere Belief. That collapses the justification/truth matrix and you lose two independent epistemic distinctions.

* The justification gap. A justified false belief is epistemically good in the sense that it is justified, but it is not Knowledge because it is false. With only Knowledge vs Belief as states the justified false belief is forced into the Belief cell together with every unjustified false belief. You therefore have no epistemic state for ‘justified belief’ as such, and in particular no way to mark the difference in epistemic merit between a justified false belief and an unjustified false belief.

* The truth gap. An unjustified true belief is true, but it is not Knowledge because it is unjustified. With only Knowledge vs Belief as states the unjustified true belief is forced into the Belief cell together with every false belief, justified or not. You therefore have no epistemic state for ‘true belief’ as such, and in particular no way to mark the difference in epistemic merit between a true unjustified belief and a false unjustified belief.

On the JTB map Justified True Belief is Knowledge and everything else is just Belief. That is why you have to treat justified false belief and unjustified true belief as epistemically on a par with unjustified false belief, even though the first is a good belief that happens to be false and the second is a lucky true belief that happens to be unjustified. That is the classic justified-false-belief and unjustified-true-belief objection to the JTB reduction of epistemic status to Knowledge vs Belief.

well known regress / circularity problem for the analysis of justification
and the consequent loss of a place for justified false belief / unjustified
true belief in a two-state taxonomy.
public_text.12:
With Knowledge = Justified True Belief and Belief as the only residual
category the state “mere belief’’ is forced to do all the work that is left over
from JTB. That makes Belief a heterogenous dump and it removes any
epistemic place for two intuitively distinct situations.

1. Justified false belief, JFB. A belief can be properly justified and yet
false. On JTB it is not Knowledge because the truth condition fails, so with
only Knowledge / Belief as options it has to be counted as mere Belief.
Hence justified beliefs that are false are lumped together with unjustified,
irrational beliefs. We lose any way of marking the epistemic value of
justification when truth is absent.

2. Unjustified true belief, UTB. A belief can be true by luck or accident
and yet be wholly unjustified. On JTB it is not Knowledge because the
justification condition fails, so with only Knowledge / Belief as options it
has to be counted as mere Belief. Hence a lucky true belief is lumped
together with false beliefs. We lose any way of marking the epistemic defect
of lack of justification when truth is present.

In effect Belief has to be both justified and unjustified and both true and
false at once. Knowledge is thereby made too narrow – it excludes
justified false beliefs we want to count as epistemically good – and Belief
is made too broad – it conflates lucky true beliefs with bad false beliefs
and justified false beliefs with unjustified false beliefs. That is the
truth-gap / justification-gap that remains even once Gettier cases are set
aside.
public_text.4:
Under JTB the space of doxastic attitude + truth-value is in principle 2x2

Justified / Unjustified x True / False

JTB identifies one of the four cells with Knowledge

J T = Knowledge
J F = ?
U T = ?
U F = ?

If the only attitudinal kinds you allow are Knowledge and Belief then J F, U T and U F all have to be classified as mere Belief. That collapses the justification/truth matrix and you lose two independent epistemic distinctions.

* The justification gap. A justified false belief is epistemically good in the sense that it is justified, but it is not Knowledge because it is false. With only Knowledge vs Belief as states the justified false belief is forced into the Belief cell together with every unjustified false belief. You therefore have no epistemic state for ‘justified belief’ as such, and in particular no way to mark the difference in epistemic merit between a justified false belief and an unjustified false belief.

* The truth gap. An unjustified true belief is true, but it is not Knowledge because it is unjustified. With only Knowledge vs Belief as states the unjustified true belief is forced into the Belief cell together with every false belief, justified or not. You therefore have no epistemic state for ‘true belief’ as such, and in particular no way to mark the difference in epistemic merit between a true unjustified belief and a false unjustified belief.

On the JTB map Justified True Belief is Knowledge and everything else is just Belief. That is why you have to treat justified false belief and unjustified true belief as epistemically on a par with unjustified false belief, even though the first is a good belief that happens to be false and the second is a lucky true belief that happens to be unjustified. That is the classic justified-false-belief and unjustified-true-belief objection to the JTB reduction of epistemic status to Knowledge vs Belief.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question restricts the inventory to Knowledge = JTB and Belief as residual, so every non-K state is forced into B. With J and T independently variable we have four cells J T, J ¬T, ¬J T, ¬J ¬T. JTB identifies only J T B with Knowledge; J ¬T B, ¬J T B and ¬J ¬T B all collapse into mere Belief.

The dominant convergence in round 0 is that this coarse-graining erases two independently interesting non-knowledge cells:

* Justified false belief, J ∧ ¬T ∧ B. On JTB it is not Knowledge because it fails truth, so with only K/B it must be counted as mere Belief. A rationally well grounded false belief is therefore indistinguishable from an arbitrary/unjustified false belief. The epistemic value of justification is invisible once truth is absent; justified falsity has no distinct home.

* Unjustified true belief, ¬J ∧ T ∧ B. On JTB it is not Knowledge because it fails justification, so with only K/B it must be counted as mere Belief. A lucky/accidental true belief is therefore indistinguishable from justified false belief and from unjustified false belief. The alethic value of truth is invisible once justification is absent; lucky truth has no distinct home.

Hence Belief becomes the heterogeneous disjunction J∧¬T∧B ∨ ¬J∧T∧B ∨ ¬J∧¬T∧B, losing independent tracking of justification and truth. This is described variously as the justification gap / truth gap and as the independence problem of J and T.

A related formal pressure noted by colleagues 10-11 is how J itself can be cashed out on a B/K only inventory. Cashed out by further beliefs it yields an infinite regress of justifiers; cashed out by knowledge it makes J(p) depend on K(q) which itself contains a belief in need of justification, yielding circularity/dogmatism or an arbitrary foundational stop. That regress/circularity is presented as the formal expression of the coarse-graining.

Disagreement/variation: colleagues 1,5,7,9,13,14 frame the problem as circular truth-verification and non-arbitrary justification standards that cannot be reduced to B/K without external criteria. Colleagues 10-11 foreground regress/circularity, colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,12 foreground the loss of distinct states for justified false belief and unjustified true belief. The two accounts are compatible: the loss of distinct states is the taxonomy effect of the regress/circularity constraint.

Current belief: the two core non-Gettier problems under a strict K/B inventory are the disappearance of a state for justified false belief and the disappearance of a state for unjustified true belief, i.e. the inability to keep apart epistemic virtue of justification from truth absence and truth presence from justification absence. Whether to phrase that as regress/circularity of justification or as coarse-graining is a matter of presentation; the content is the same.

Unresolved: how much weight to give to the explicit regress vs circularity formulation versus the taxonomy coarse-graining formulation when the final answer is required; and whether the question expects regress/circularity as the two problems rather than the two collapsed cells.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion centers on what is lost when the epistemic inventory is restricted to Knowledge = Justified True Belief and the residual category Belief.

There is broad agreement that with only K and B the 2×2 truth × justification matrix collapses: JTB → K, and ¬K → B. Belief becomes the heterogeneous disjunction J∧¬T∧B ∨ ¬J∧T∧B ∨ ¬J∧¬T∧B.

The dominant formulation repeated by Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,12 is the coarse-graining / independence loss:
* Justified false belief. J∧¬T∧B is not Knowledge because it is false, so on a K/B only taxonomy it must be counted as mere Belief. Justified falsity is lumped with unjustified falsity; the epistemic merit of justification is erased once truth fails.
* Unjustified true belief. ¬J∧T∧B is not Knowledge because it lacks justification, so it must also be counted as mere Belief. A lucky/accidental true belief is lumped with justified false belief and with unjustified false belief; the alethic merit of truth is erased once justification fails.

Hence the taxonomy cannot mark off a justified belief that is false as a sui generis rational-but-false state, nor a true belief that is unjustified as a sui generis lucky-but-unwarranted state. Knowledge is too narrow and Belief is too broad.

A second, linked line stresses the internal grounding of the J-clause given the same inventory. Colleagues 10,11 note that justification of p has to be cashed out in the only available states, belief or knowledge.
* If J(p) is cashed out by a further belief B(q), J(q) is required, etc., giving the familiar regress of justification with no non-infinite B-chain to ground p.
* If the chain is stopped by making the justifier itself a knowledge state K(q), K(q) is B(q)&T(q)&J(q), so justification of p depends on justification of q and you are back in regress, or else you close the chain dogmatically/foundationally with an unjustified basic belief/knowledge.

Colleagues 1,5,7,9,14,13 phrase this as the need for an external/non-epistemic criterion for truth and for a non-arbitrary standard for justification, and as circularity in verifying truth without already presupposing knowledge. That is the formal expression of the coarse-graining: justification and truth cannot be independently tracked in a two-state taxonomy, so J either regresses or is stipulated.

Unresolved tension: some colleagues present the regress/circularity as the primary problem, others present the JFB/UTB indistinguishability as the primary problem. They appear interdependent: the lack of an independent justified-belief state is what forces the regress/dogmatism dilemma and what makes Belief a heterogeneous dump.

I am keeping both the justification-gap / truth-gap collapse of JFB and UTB into bare Belief, and the regress/circularity/dogmatism problem for cashing out J in terms of only B/K, as the two closely linked non-Gettier difficulties under the K/B restriction.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The round-0 discussion clusters around the consequence of forcing the four J×T combinations into only the two boxes Knowledge = J∧T∧B and Belief = ¬Knowledge.

A strong majority — Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,12 — frames the problem as coarse-graining / loss of independence of justification and truth. With only K/B available, every non-K state is lumped into Belief:
* J∧¬T∧B = justified false belief must be called mere Belief. The epistemic virtue of justification is erased once truth fails; justified falsity is indistinguishable from unjustified falsity.
* ¬J∧T∧B = unjustified true belief must also be called mere Belief. The alethic virtue of truth is erased once justification fails; lucky/accidental true belief is indistinguishable from false belief and from justified false belief.

Belief therefore becomes the heterogeneous disjunction J&~T&B ∨ ~J&T&B ∨ ~J&~T&B, so the taxonomy cannot mark off a justified but false state nor a true but unjustified state. This is described as the justification gap and the truth gap, the independence problem of J and T distinct from Gettier.

A second strand — Colleagues 10,11,1,7,5,9,14 — reformulates the same inventory limit meta-epistemically:
* Justification cannot be cashed out in the allowed vocabulary. If J(p) is to be a further epistemic state it must be B(q) or K(q). B(q) requires J(q) → regress of justification; stopping the regress with K(q) re-introduces J(q) and yields circularity/dogmatism or an arbitrary foundational belief.
* Truth cannot be independently verified from within the K/B inventory without smuggling in an external criterion, so truth-checking risks collapsing into further belief/knowledge attributions.

Disagreement / nuance noted:
* Some colleagues stress regress/circularity and truth verification as the two problems; others stress the two missing cells justified false belief and unjustified true belief.
* Colleagues 13,14,5,7 also mention circular truth assessment and arbitrary justification standards, which overlap with the regress point.

Current working understanding: The inventory limit makes Belief a grab-bag and removes an epistemic place for justified false belief and for unjustified true belief. That is the core non-Gettier difficulty; the regress/circularity formulation is the formal expression of the same limitation. Unresolved is whether the examiner wants the formulation in terms of the two missing cells or in terms of justification regress + truth verification.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is split between a regress/circularity diagnosis and a taxonomy-coarsening diagnosis, both stemming from the restriction to only Knowledge and Belief as epistemic states.

With K(p) := B(p) & T(p) & J(p) and only K/B available, every non-K state must be classified as mere Belief. That forces Belief to be heterogeneous: J&T&B = K; J&~T&B, ~J&T&B, ~J&~T&B all = Belief.

The dominant coarse-graining claim, made by Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,12:
1. Justified false belief problem / justification gap. A belief can be properly justified yet false. The epistemic merit of justification is invisible once truth fails; there is no distinct state for ‘justified but false’.
2. Unjustified true belief problem / truth gap. A belief can be true by luck/accident with no justification. JTB makes it non-K, so it is also forced into Belief, lumped with justified false belief and unjustified false belief. The alethic merit of truth is invisible once justification fails; there is no distinct state for ‘true but unwarranted’.

Hence Belief becomes J&~T&B ∨ ~J&T&B ∨ ~J&~T&B, and justification and truth can no longer be tracked independently of the K/B dichotomy.

Unresolved tension: whether the two problems should be framed as the regress/circularity of justification and the non-verifiability of truth within K/B, or as the concrete loss of distinct epistemic places for justified false belief and unjustified true belief. 12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion so far converges on the coarse-graining that follows from restricting the epistemic inventory to Knowledge = J ∧ T ∧ B and Belief as the sole residual category.

With only K and B the 2×2 J×T matrix collapses:
* J ∧ T ∧ B = Knowledge
* J ∧ ¬T ∧ B, ¬J ∧ T ∧ B, ¬J ∧ ¬T ∧ B all = Belief

Most of the strongest consensus is around two non-Gettier cells that become indistinguishable from plain, unwarranted false belief:

1. Justified false belief, J ∧ ¬T ∧ B. On JTB it is not Knowledge because it fails the truth condition, so with a K/B only taxonomy it must be counted as mere Belief. A rationally warranted but false belief is therefore lumped with unjustified false belief; the epistemic virtue of justification is erased once truth is absent. This is the “justified but wrong / false lemma” difficulty.

2. Unjustified true belief, ¬J ∧ T ∧ B. On JTB it is not Knowledge because it fails the justification condition, so it too must be counted as mere Belief. A lucky/accidental true belief is therefore lumped with justified false belief and with unjustified false belief; the alethic virtue of truth is erased once justification is absent.
